bridges.description: Show that the existence of a moral arena favors a morally perfect theistic hypothesis strongly enough to support the motion.
Compare how expected the observed universe and moral agents are under theism and atheism using likelihood ratios.
Connect biological information and function to intelligent agency through claimed cause-and-effect regularities.
Argue that contingent reality ultimately requires an eternal necessary ground and that God is the best candidate.
Show that the presented observations do not distinguish God from non-God alternatives and therefore do not establish the motion.
Use unknown natural causes or a naturalistic-pantheist comparison model to match the explanatory work assigned to God.
Challenge the numerical priors and the restriction of the theistic comparison class used in the Bayesian case.
Argue that involuntary suffering and compelled existence conflict with the morally perfect God under discussion.
Require discriminating, observable predictions before treating an explanation as evidence for God.

sections.title: Bayesian comparison and priors
sections.rationale: The main affirmative case is explicitly a likelihood-ratio argument, and much of the direct clash concerns priors, comparison classes and what counts as evidence.

sections.title: Cosmic conditions and necessary origins
sections.rationale: Fine-tuning, the origin of a life-permitting universe and the proposed necessary ground supply major links between the observed cosmos and the motion.

sections.title: Explanatory rivals and empirical testing
sections.rationale: The debate repeatedly asks whether non-God alternatives are genuine rivals and what would discriminate among explanations.

sections.title: Biological information and design
sections.rationale: Biological information, functional sequences and design detection are a substantial evidential strand and the focus of extended cross-examination.

sections.title: Moral arena, embodiment and divine goodness
sections.rationale: The affirmative likelihood depends on divine goodness and embodied moral agency, while the negative presents moral incompatibility and parity objections.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: Evidence favors a hypothesis when the evidence is more probable on that hypothesis than on its antithesis.
moves.warrant: The odds form of Bayes' theorem multiplies prior odds by a likelihood ratio measuring how much more expected the evidence is under the hypothesis.
moves.inference: If a moral arena is substantially more expected on theism than atheism, its existence raises the posterior probability of theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the smallest continuous opening passage that introduces the odds form, defines the Bayes factor and states the comparison the argument will use.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the odds form of Bayes theorem
a moral arena given theism is greater
moves.attributionRationale: McLatchie's opening begins after an explicit named handoff and remains a continuous solo statement.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies the governing method for the entire affirmative case.

burdenContact.rationale: It defines the likelihood comparison by which the moral arena is meant to support theism.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: A morally good God has a plausible reason to create a community of embodied agents capable of morally significant action.
moves.warrant: McLatchie says an all-good God is not unlikely to bring about great goods and that the greatest goods require such a community.
moves.inference: A moral arena receives a non-negligible likelihood under the morally perfect theistic hypothesis.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with the theistic likelihood question and ends after the stated one-percent estimate and its moral-goodness rationale.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: all good God is not unlikely
community of embodied moral agents
moves.attributionRationale: This is a continuous part of McLatchie's named opening; corrupted caption wording is preserved and not treated as a speaking defect.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the principal warrant for the affirmative side of the likelihood ratio.

burdenContact.rationale: It links the morally perfect God under discussion to the observed moral arena.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: A moral arena requires a temporally finite, law-governed and life-permitting universe whose conditions are highly restricted.
moves.warrant: McLatchie cites the cosmological constant, initial low entropy and other physical ratios as examples of conditions that must fall in narrow life-permitting ranges.
moves.inference: He assigns a low likelihood to reaching the cosmic preconditions of moral agency under atheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This long opening unit is kept intact because it states the life-permitting requirement, supplies several independent physical examples rather than one isolated illustration, and ends with the speaker's conservative atheistic-likelihood assignment at events 355–363; cutting it would detach that assignment from much of its stated warrant.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you need specifically a life permitting universe
our universe is balanced on a Razors Edge
moves.attributionRationale: McLatchie's uninterrupted opening covers this whole evidential unit; numerical caption uncertainty is preserved and will not itself be judged.
moves.importanceRationale: Cosmic fine-tuning is a major factor in the affirmative probability product.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the first major claimed low-probability condition under atheism.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: Functional protein sequences are presented as extremely rare within the space of possible amino-acid sequences.
moves.warrant: McLatchie describes the combinatorial sequence space and cites an experiment estimating that stable functional folds occupy a very small part of it.
moves.inference: The rarity of functional proteins is presented as making life's origin unlikely under unguided atheistic processes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This narrowed passage begins with the ratio of functional to nonfunctional protein sequences, gives the cited experimental estimate and needle-in-a-haystack warrant, and ends with the conservative likelihood assignment.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: functional protein sequences relative to the non-functional gibberish
a needle and a haystack problem
moves.attributionRationale: This is within McLatchie's continuous opening. Recognition-corrupted technical terms and numbers are not repaired or treated as errors.
moves.importanceRationale: The origin of life is one of the main multiplicative steps and later grounds the design exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the biological pattern for which intelligent causation is later proposed.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: Multiplying the assigned upper bounds for the required atheistic steps makes a moral arena extremely improbable on atheism.
moves.warrant: The preceding chain includes cosmic origins, fine-tuning, life, cellular machinery, multicellularity, consciousness and moral sensibility, each assigned a conservative upper bound.
moves.inference: Because the asserted theistic likelihood is higher, the moral arena is said to provide strong evidence for theism and overcome a very low prior.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the concluding calculation and inference, beginning with the last two factors and ending with the motion-level conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: multiply the upper bound of all these numbers together
the moral arena is strong evidence for theism
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is the conclusion of McLatchie's uninterrupted opening; the numerical posterior is recorded without independent correction or error attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This aggregates the affirmative premises into its motion-level conclusion.

burdenContact.rationale: It states how the cumulative likelihood comparison is meant to affirm God's existence.

moves.speaker: Tom Jump
moves.claim: An observation is not evidence specifically for God when many non-God explanations fit it equally well.
moves.warrant: Jump uses a two-pound box to argue that weight alone does not discriminate a rabbit from many other contents and extends the analogy to cosmic origins, fine-tuning and morality.
moves.inference: Without evidence that selects God over alternatives, those observations do not establish the motion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This narrowed passage contains the complete two-pound-box analogy, its application to cosmic origins, fine-tuning and morality, and the resulting underdetermination claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there needs to be some kind of evidence
equally explained by the non God
moves.attributionRationale: Jump's opening follows an explicit named handoff and remains a solo statement.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the negative's main motion-level standard and organizes most of his later replies.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the evidence does not distinguish the motion from non-God rivals.

moves.speaker: Tom Jump
moves.claim: The origin and fine-tuning of the universe can be assigned to unknown natural laws or a naturalistic-pantheist model as readily as to God.
moves.warrant: Jump proposes an eternal natural basis, undiscovered unifying constraints and natural moral laws as comparison explanations.
moves.inference: If those non-God models can match the observations, the observations do not preferentially support God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage lists the non-God models for cosmic origins, fine-tuning and morality and continues through the completed conclusion that these alternatives leave the cited observations without God-specific evidential force.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: explained by an all-powerful eternal things
explained by non God alternatives
moves.attributionRationale: This is a continuous portion of Jump's opening; the comparison model is represented as an argumentative alternative, not silently converted into his personal belief.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the chief alternative used against the cosmic likelihood case.

burdenContact.rationale: It constructs non-God comparison explanations for the affirmative observations.

moves.speaker: Tom Jump
moves.claim: Because neither unknown supernatural nor unknown natural causes have been discovered, neither side may stipulate limits that favor its preferred explanation.
moves.warrant: Jump argues that identifying an unknown cause as supernatural would contradict its being unidentified, and says the same constraint applies to unknown natural causes.
moves.inference: Whatever explanatory possibility is assigned to God can also be assigned to an unknown natural force until discriminating evidence is available.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with the concession that a supernatural reality is possible and ends with the stated parity between God and unknown natural forces.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: both the supernatural and the unknown natural are undiscovered
anything that God can explain
moves.attributionRationale: This is still Jump's uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It provides the general parity principle behind the negative's rival explanations.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that unknown natural causes cannot be excluded merely by assigning capacities to God.

moves.speaker: Tom Jump
moves.claim: A morally good and all-powerful creator would not force persons into a world containing involuntary suffering without consent.
moves.warrant: Jump characterizes compelled existence for another's purposes and a forced heaven-or-hell choice as forms of slavery and therefore immoral.
moves.inference: The described world is incompatible with the morally perfect creator invoked by the affirmative case.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage contains the complete nonconsent argument from its conditional premise through the claimed incompatibility.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a world without involuntary suffering

moves.attributionRationale: Jump delivers this continuously near the end of his opening; the caption's later missing negation is avoided in the selected exact spans.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the moral character central to McLatchie's theistic likelihood.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the actual moral arena conflicts with the morally perfect God proposed.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: The debate's motion concerns God's existence in a minimal generic sense, not the additional claims of Christianity.
moves.warrant: McLatchie distinguishes the exact motion from the separate question whether the Christian God exists.
moves.inference: Jump's specifically Christian objections do not by themselves answer the affirmative's generic theistic case.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the opening unit of McLatchie's first rebuttal, from his identification of Jump's claim through the scope distinction.

moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the burden and prevents a narrower Christian target from replacing the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It limits the affirmative conclusion to generic theism.

responseComponents.description: It argues that a specifically Christian incompatibility claim does not by itself resolve the generic motion.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: Evidence may raise a hypothesis's probability even when it is also compatible with other hypotheses.
moves.warrant: McLatchie says a box's weight can weakly support a rabbit hypothesis and that eliminating one rival redistributes probability among those remaining.
moves.inference: The existence of alternatives does not entail that the moral-arena evidence provides no support for theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the complete rabbit reply and the probability-redistribution explanation ending in the epistemological disagreement.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it would still be evidence for the hypothesis

moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the negative's core definition of evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends probabilistic confirmation despite underdetermination.

responseComponents.description: It denies that equal compatibility automatically removes all evidential support and reframes support as probability raising.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: Competing explanations should be compared by explanatory power, scope and prior plausibility rather than by fit to a single observation alone.
moves.warrant: McLatchie argues that theism unifies varied data under one hypothesis, whereas alternatives may need multiple independent hypotheses, and he questions the necessity and clarity of naturalistic pantheism.
moves.inference: A merely possible rival does not reach explanatory parity unless it also performs well on those comparison criteria.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This unit starts with the explicit comparison criteria and ends after applying scope, plausibility and contingency to the pantheist rival.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the different hypotheses are adjudicated

moves.importanceRationale: It states the affirmative method for comparing the central rival explanations.

burdenContact.rationale: It adds scope and plausibility constraints to the likelihood comparison.

responseComponents.description: It requires the naturalistic-pantheist model to match more than bare possibility.
It argues that an unspecified unknown does not automatically share theism's scope and plausibility.

moves.inference: If that leaner non-God model can be made explanatorily equal, the observations do not favor the more property-rich theistic model.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Jump's direct response to the scope objection, including his definition and parsimony comparison.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the one and only criteria I'm using

moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the affirmative likelihood numerator at the model-selection level.
